This Hebrew word means “divided,” describing the action of separating something into parts. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person or thing. This Hebrew word describes expressing deep grief aloud—“lamented” or “wail.” It refers to an outward cry of sorrow rather than a silent feeling, so it can describe people mourning together or giving voice to distress. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense is audible mourning.

The name occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 12 verses, and is used consistently as “Amasa.” Its occurrences are concentrated in 2 Samuel, with additional appearances in 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and 2 Chronicles. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about the person named.

Anani is a personal name used to identify an individual, rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, and the English rendering preserves it as “Anani.” Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise place in that genealogy cannot be explained further; the lexical sense is simply the individual’s name. This is its normal use in the Hebrew corpus.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “prudence,” the quality of approaching situations with careful, purposeful judgment. It describes a useful kind of wisdom that helps a person recognize how to act wisely rather than thoughtlessly. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Joshua, and Proverbs. In Proverbs, prudence is presented as something that can be given, learned, and found alongside wisdom, showing its practical role in guiding conduct.

Athlai is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Athlai.” It identifies one individual in the Old Testament and appears only once, in Ezra 10:28. Because this is a proper name rather than a descriptive word, its main function is to identify the person who bears it, not to express an action, quality, or general idea. The name’s precise significance beyond identifying that individual is not stated by the available biblical material.

In the Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in Exodus, where it is associated with crafted gold objects and appears within instructions or commands concerning those objects. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes a place as “unwalled,” indicating that it lacks surrounding walls. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, each time referring to a settled place rather than to an action or quality of character. Its use in Esther, Ezekiel, and Zechariah shows the word’s consistent basic sense: a community or inhabited place not enclosed by walls. The precise force in any verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a place that is unwalled.

This Hebrew word means “foot,” referring to the body part used for standing and walking. It functions as a noun naming that part of the body. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, so its basic meaning remains consistent while the surrounding sentence determines how the foot is being mentioned. The word appears from Exodus through Jeremiah and is rendered “foot” in the available English renderings.

This Hebrew word means “form.” It functions as a naming word for a form, identifying what something is like in its visible or described shape. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Daniel, at Daniel 2:31 and Daniel 3:25. Since no surrounding verse text is available here, its precise force in each sentence must be understood from the immediate context, but the central meaning remains “form.”

This Hebrew noun refers to “princes,” people recognized as holding governing authority. It is used of prominent leaders in passages addressing kings, rulers, and those who exercise power over others. The word appears six times in the Old Testament, from Judges through Habakkuk, showing a consistent connection with people who occupy elevated positions of rule. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a person of princely authority.

This Hebrew word refers to “knees,” the joints connecting the thighs and lower legs. It functions as a bodily term naming those parts, and its approved meaning is clear even though no fuller definition is available. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 5:6. The precise force of the word in that verse belongs to its surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is simply “knees.”

This Hebrew verb means “impoverish.” It describes an action that brings poverty or severe lack upon someone or something. As an action word, it points to what is done to a person, household, city, or possession, rather than naming poverty as a condition by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Jeremiah 5:17 and Malachi 1:4. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “Shunites,” the designation for a particular people group. It functions as a plural name for people associated with the name Shun, rather than as a general description of character, action, or condition. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 26:15. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that passage must be understood from the larger context, but its basic meaning is the name of this people group.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a thought or something conceived in the mind. It functions as the object of actions such as making, declaring, and forming, presenting thought as something that can be expressed or brought forth. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 4:13. Its association there is with creation, showing thought within a passage about God’s creative activity.

This Hebrew verb means “find.” It expresses the action of finding someone or something, and its wording functions as a predicate in the sentence rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 18 times, with occurrences in Ezra and Daniel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to the “Shumathites,” a named group or family designation. It functions as a plural identifying term rather than a description of an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 2:53, and is rendered “Shumathites” in the available English renderings. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding genealogy, but its basic role is to identify people belonging to this named group.

This Hebrew word means “legs.” It functions as a noun naming a part of the body. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 2:33, and its consistent English rendering there is “legs.” Because the verse text is not included here, this entry explains the word’s ordinary meaning rather than the specific significance it carries in that passage. Its meaning is therefore clear at the basic lexical level, while the surrounding verse determines how the reference is being used.

This Hebrew word commonly means “that” and functions as a connector within a sentence. It links a statement to a person, thing, time, or action being identified or described, helping relate one part of the sentence to another. It is very frequent in the Old Testament, occurring 5,500 times, so its precise English expression depends on the sentence where it appears. Its normal role is grammatical rather than a standalone description or action.

This Hebrew word refers to something wild or untamed. It appears twice in the Old Testament, with both occurrences rendered “wild.” The word is used in Deuteronomy 14:5 and Isaiah 51:20, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes in each passage. Its central meaning remains the idea of being outside domestication or ordinary cultivated order.

Asarelah is a personal name, identifying one individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 25:2, and is rendered “Asarelah.” Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name itself is the clearest meaning available: it functions as a person’s identifying name in that passage.

This Hebrew word describes the action to “mark.” It functions as an action word, referring to placing or making a distinguishing sign. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, across two verses, so its basic sense is narrow and specific rather than broad or frequent. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation.

This Hebrew word means “sheriffs.” It is a noun used as a title for authorities or officials. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Daniel 3:2–3, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. The word identifies a recognized office rather than describing an action, feeling, or quality. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic meaning remains a title for sheriffs.

Tartan is a Hebrew name rendered “Tartan.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only twice: once in 2 Kings 18:17 and once in Isaiah 20:1. Because no short definition beyond this stable name rendering is available, its ordinary meaning is best understood as the personal designation “Tartan.” The surrounding verse text is needed to explain that person’s specific role in either passage.
